questions.prompt: Which order matches the suggested flow for a first demo, after the up-front contract?

options.text: Discovery, recap, client side, back end, price, close
Client side, back end, discovery, recap, price, close
Recap, client side, discovery, back end, close, price
Back end, discovery, client side, recap, close, price

questions.reveal: Find the need, say it back, show the client side and then their day, and only then price and close.

questions.prompt: Fifteen minutes in, the co-owner joins the call. What should you do before you go on?

options.text: Keep going so the first owner doesn't lose the thread
Restart the whole demo from the beginning for them
Ask them to watch the recording later instead
Recap where you are and agree what's left for the call

questions.reveal: Whenever a decision-maker joins late, re-set the plan so they know what's been covered and how the call ends.

questions.prompt: In our strongest first demos, about how long did discovery run before the first screen?

options.text: About 1 to 2 minutes, then straight to the screen
About 5 to 10 minutes, with open questions
About 15 to 20 minutes, the first half of the call
About 25 to 30 minutes, most of the whole call

questions.reveal: Long enough to learn the pain, its cost, the spend and who decides. When it was cut to a question or two, the must-haves came out late.

questions.prompt: Fifty minutes in, your next meeting starts and the owner asks, “So how do we go from here?” What would have prevented this?

options.text: Showing fewer features so the demo ran a bit faster
Sending the agenda by email the day before the call
Agreeing the time and how it ends in the first minutes
Booking a longer slot so there was time for questions

questions.reveal: An up-front contract covers how long the call runs and how it ends, so the next step is planned, not improvised.

questions.prompt: Early in discovery, the owner says onboarding with her current software was “messy.” What's your best next move?

options.text: Say, “Tell me about that,” and let her walk you through it
Promise that Momence onboarding is much easier than that
Move on and ask how many classes she runs each week
Share your screen and show the onboarding checklist

questions.reveal: Stay on the pain. Her story is what you'll answer later in the demo.

questions.prompt: Which set belongs in discovery, before you share your screen?

options.text: Their logo, brand colors, website and social accounts
Current tools, the pain and its cost, spend, who decides
Which features they want and which add-ons they’ll buy
Their staff list, class schedule and membership prices

questions.reveal: What they use, what isn't working and what it costs, what they pay and who decides. The rest comes later.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the short recap between discovery and the demo?

options.text: A summary of every add-on and what each one includes
A list of every feature you plan to show, in your order
Their top needs in their words, and what you'll show first
A reminder of how long Momence has worked with studios

questions.reveal: Say it back, ask what you missed, and name the order, starting with their top need.

questions.prompt: You ask whether she wants to grow or mostly fix problems. She says, “Just fix the booking headaches.” How does that shape the demo?

options.text: Lead with booking, and keep marketing short or skip it
Lead with marketing, since growth always follows later
Show every part equally so she can decide on her own
Skip the demo and go straight to price and the close

questions.reveal: Her answer tells you where to spend the time. Marketing can wait until growth is a goal.

questions.prompt: The owner's pain is that clients need too many clicks to book a session. Where do you start the screen share?

options.text: On the dashboard, to show how the business runs
On the reports, to show what clients are booking
On a client booking on a live studio's checkout
On the marketing suite, to show the big upgrade

questions.reveal: Start where it hurts and count the clicks with them.

questions.prompt: Which front-end moment was among the strongest in our demos?

options.text: A full tour of every checkout setting and option
Their own booking flow next to a Momence checkout
A slide that compares feature lists across vendors
The admin dashboard shown before any client screen

questions.reveal: Seeing their own login walls and redirects next to a one-page checkout makes the difference concrete.

questions.prompt: During the back end, the owner says, “Paying for friends is a big deal for us.” You were about to show guest passes. What do you do?

options.text: Show guest passes first, then come back to it later
Say it's easy and keep going to finish the tour
Note it for onboarding and move to the schedule
Stop, ask what happens today, and show that flow

questions.reveal: When they say something matters, stay there. The next screen can wait.

questions.prompt: The owner asks whether Momence can always fill single clients into a couples room last. You're not sure. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, since most room setups can be configured
Say what you know works, and confirm the rest after
Say no, so you don't risk overpromising anything
Move on and hope it doesn't come up again later

questions.reveal: Show the closest fit, say what you don't know, and confirm it. Guessing either way costs trust.

questions.prompt: An owner gets few client messages but loses leads who start to book and don't finish. What should you show her?

options.text: Sequences that follow up on abandoned checkouts
The AI agent answering routine inbox messages
A branded app with her logo in the app store
Point of sale and the card reader at the desk

questions.reveal: Abandoned checkouts become leads, and sequences follow up with them automatically.

questions.prompt: When do marketing and the AI belong in a first demo?

options.text: Always, since they're the biggest upgrades we sell
Only after they've signed, during their onboarding
Only if the owner asks to see them by name first
When they fit what the owner said in discovery

questions.reveal: Growth goals, lost leads or a busy inbox make them relevant. Otherwise mention them and move on.

questions.prompt: The demo is done and you're about to price. What should come right before the number?

options.text: A list of every feature included in the quote
A reminder of the offer that ends this month
A question about which add-ons they like most
A short recap of what landed, in their words

questions.reveal: The recap reminds them what they're paying for, so the price lands on value they've seen.

questions.prompt: The owner pays for a booking tool and a separate texting tool. How do you set up the price comparison?

options.text: Compare to the booking tool, since it's the main one
Skip the comparison and show the quote alone
Ask both costs early and compare against the total
Compare to the cheapest competitor in their area

questions.reveal: An all-in-one replaces both tools, so the fair comparison is their total spend.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a trial close?

options.text: “Do you have any other questions about the features?”
“Does what you saw solve the problems you told me?”
“Would you like me to send you a recap by email?”
“Should I show you the rest of the marketing suite?”

questions.reveal: It checks whether the demo did its job and surfaces what's left before you ask for the decision.

questions.prompt: Mid-demo, an owner mentions two local studios have asked her to buy them. What's the best move?

options.text: Note it and come back to it if she raises it again
Quote three locations now so she sees the full cost
Ask how they'd be owned and run, then show locations
Tell her a branded app is a must for more locations

questions.reveal: How the locations are owned and run decides the setup and the quote. Ask before you show anything.

questions.prompt: You start a follow-up call. The owner emailed a list of questions, with one marked as her deal-breaker. What do you cover first?

options.text: Her list in the order she wrote it, top to bottom
A short recap demo of everything from last time
The pricing, since it's what decides most deals
Her deal-breaker, then the rest of her list

questions.reveal: Prove the deal-breaker first. If it fails, the rest doesn't matter. If it works, the rest goes faster.

questions.prompt: A pre-open owner starts presales in January and opens in February. What fits her best?

options.text: Memberships that activate on first use
A branded app before the doors open
The AI agent to answer her inbox now
Payroll reports for her future staff

questions.reveal: She can sell founding memberships now, and they start when clients first come in.
